headline: Spring tides fire the Sound as bass crash bunker pods in 68-degree water
subhead: New moon currents push bait against structure while fluke move shallow on warming bottom.
body_markdown:
The new moon that peaked Friday delivered exactly what I expected — screaming currents that turned the Central Sound into a feeding machine. Water temps hit 68 degrees across my beat, from the Norwalk Islands to Port Jeff, and that magic number has everything switched on.

I've been watching the bunker schools thicken all week, and these spring tides are doing exactly what they're supposed to do — flushing bait out of the harbors and stacking it against the structure where bass wait. The Stratford Shoal rip has been producing consistent fish on the outgoing, especially that last two hours when the current really gets moving. White bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range are the ticket here — cast up-current, let them sink to the bottom, then work them back with slow lifts. The bass are hitting on the drop, classic ambush behavior when they're positioned on structure facing into the flow.

What's got me excited is how the bait is positioning. The spearing are thick along the Connecticut shoreline from Stamford to New Haven, and I'm seeing good marks on the fishfinder in 25 to 35 feet of water. This is where the fluke action has really turned on. The warming bottom — we're seeing 68 degrees in the shallows versus 64 in deeper water — is pulling flatfish up onto the edges where they're easier to target.

For fluke, I'm running 3/4-ounce white bucktails with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets, dragged slow on the drift. The key is reading the bottom first — use your electronics to find those drop-offs from 15 feet down to 30. That's where they're stacked. The Norwalk Islands have been particularly good, especially the channel edges on the north side where the depth breaks from shallow flats to deeper holes.

The current situation is textbook for this lunar phase. These big spring tides take time to get moving — sometimes an hour after the tide change before you feel real flow — but when they hit, they're screaming. That's when the baitfish lose control and the predators capitalize. I've been timing my trips for that sweet spot two hours into the outgoing when everything lines up.

Porgies are showing up as a bonus, especially around Middle Ground Light where the structure holds them in 30 to 40 feet. Small pieces of clam on high-low rigs are producing nice keepers mixed in with the usual shorts. The bigger porgies seem to move in when the current eases, so don't write off the slack periods entirely.

One pattern I'm tracking closely is how the thermal structure is setting up. That 4-degree gradient between shallow and deep water is creating edges that concentrate bait. The bass are using these temperature breaks like highways, following them as they hunt. When you find 68-degree water next to 64-degree water, that's where you want to focus your efforts.

Looking ahead, we're moving into the heart of summer fishing with water temps climbing toward the 70-degree mark. This should push the bigger bass deeper during the day, making early morning and evening the prime windows. The bunker schools will continue to thicken, and I'm expecting the first real bluefish push any day now. Keep an eye on the bird activity — when you see terns and gulls working, that's your cue to get there fast with topwater plugs or bucktails.
